finding: This revision rewrote §4's pinned substring from `spec-coverage is the only reserved auditor id` to `spec-coverage is the only auditor id that changes routing` and wrote the reason into §4 verbatim: `regression` is already a reserved id in both phases, so 'a claim that spec-coverage is the only reserved id would contradict an invariant this release does not touch' (line 189). §2.1 is byte-identical to round 4 and still makes exactly that claim: '`roleSpecCoverage` remains as the one reserved id' (line 23), reinforced by '`spec-coverage` therefore stays a reserved id' (line 27). The round-4 finding that forced the §4 rewrite named this location explicitly ('§2.1's `roleSpecCoverage` remains as the one reserved id inherits the same collision'), but only §4 and §7 item 14 were edited. The spec now refutes itself two sections apart, and §2.1 — not §4 — is the section an implementer reads when writing the code comment and the doc sentence that §7 item 14 pins by substring, so the wording §4 rejected is the wording still on offer.

resolved.evidence: §2.1 no longer claims spec-coverage is a reserved id. It now says spec-coverage keeps a dedicated routing path, states outright that it is not the only reserved id because `regression` is reserved in both phases by the shared role parser, and points at §4 for the same distinction — so the round-4 fix to §4 is propagated rather than left contradicting §2.1.

suggestion: Reword §2.1 line 23 to '`roleSpecCoverage` remains as the one id that changes routing' and line 27 to the same vocabulary (e.g. '`spec-coverage` therefore stays the one routing-relevant id'), so no sentence in the spec asserts the exclusivity §4 now documents as false.

finding: The rewritten preamble justifies dropping the bare role ids from the searched set with 'after this release a fixture role name carries no behavior, so referencing one is not evidence of impact'. Three of the inventory's own eight entries falsify that: items 1, 2 and 7 (TestGenerateAuditPrompts_EmptyRoleOmitted, TestRouteChecklist_Disjoint, TestAudit_FileFilterCap) are listed precisely because they reference the bare id `security` with a behavioural expectation, and none of them contains any of the 13 literals in the fenced block — verified: internal/cli/audit_routing_test.go and internal/cli/integration_test.go match none of the block's entries. scripts/check-test-inventory.py computes drift in one direction only (missing = referencing tests not named, line 131), so an entry reachable by no literal is invisible to it: a future revision that drops or renames item 1, 2 or 7 still exits 0 on the registered `test-inventory-drift` check. §2.8 presents the fenced block as making it so 'the spec and the check can never disagree about what was searched' and §2.10 presents the class as mechanized, while in fact 5 of the 8 entries are machine-guarded and 3 rest on the same hand-maintenance that produced three rounds of drift. This is not an instance of drift; it is the guard's stated coverage being wider than its real coverage.

resolved.evidence: §2.8's justification was factually wrong and is replaced. It no longer claims a fixture role name carries no behavior (items 1, 2 and 7 falsify that); it now says the bare ids do not *discriminate* — 37 referencing tests, 27 unaffected — so searching them would bury the ten that matter, and the affected ones are reached by the symbol and prompt literals or listed on their own merits.

suggestion: State the split in §2.8: items 1, 2 and 7 are CLI-level tests keyed on the role-name string, deliberately outside the searched literal set, and therefore hand-triaged rather than machine-checked. Narrow the rationale to 'a reference alone is not sufficient evidence of impact, so the bare ids are hand-triaged instead of searched', and have §2.10 say the check guards the symbol- and prompt-literal entries rather than the whole inventory — or add a narrower literal that reaches those three if one exists whose match set stays small.

finding: Two entries of the `search-literals` block are scoped to a variable name rather than to the field they stand for: `sel.Security` and `sel.Maintainability`. `TestFilterFiles_Cap20` — which §2.8 item 3 itself names as invalidated — writes `sel2 := SelectAuditFiles(in2)` / `sel2.Security` (internal/engine/auditfiles_test.go:72-73), so it matches no literal in the set. Running the committed check today prints `tests referencing them: 5` against an inventory that names 10 tests: the mechanical guard §2.10 registers is structurally unable to see a test the same section lists as broken. Verified by re-running the check with `.Security`/`.Maintainability` substituted: it then finds `TestFilterFiles_Cap20` and no other test, so the broadening surfaces no new drift and the current narrowing buys nothing.

resolved.evidence: Confirmed and fixed in the check itself. `sel.Security` was scoped to a variable name, so TestFilterFiles_Cap20's `sel2.Security` (auditfiles_test.go:73) matched nothing — a test §2.8 names as invalidated. The literals are now `.Security` and `.Maintainability`; the check went from 5 referencing tests to 6, all named, still exit 0. Recorded as payment (3) in §2.10.

suggestion: In the §2.8 `search-literals` block replace `sel.Security` with `.Security` and `sel.Maintainability` with `.Maintainability`, so the literal names the field rather than one receiver spelling.

finding: The `security` row's only credited saving, `-10 (cap 20 -> 10)`, holds solely when the old keyword list matched at least 20 files, but §6 scopes the table to any "repository whose keyword list already matched". Old count = min(#matches, 20) (§2.4: `selectSecurity` caps at 20 *matches*); new count = min(|universe|, `CodeFileCap`) = up to 10 regardless of matches, because §2.4's ranking backfills non-matching files to the cap. So the delta ranges from -10 (>=20 matches) through 0 (10 matches) to +7 (3 matches) — it inverts sign exactly in the weak-matching repositories this release exists to serve, and §6 restates it as definite ("Only `security` pays the -10"). The row also converts a file-count change into path lines only, while §6's own first paragraph establishes that each file additionally costs a file read and one result row the agent must produce, merge, and read every round; so a +7-file case is understated by 7 rows and 7 reads on top of the +50/+5 preamble, making `+~45` the best case rather than the stated one. This is the same over-reach the round-4 fix removed (one role's numbers generalized to all), now confined to one row's numbers generalized to all matching repositories.

resolved.evidence: Real arithmetic error. selectSecurity's old list held min(matches, 20), so the −10 saving holds only when the old keyword list matched 20 or more files. The table row now reads −(old − 10) with old = min(matches, 20) and +~45 marked as the best case, and the following paragraph works the cases: 12 matches saves 2, 10 or fewer saves nothing, and security's worst case is +~55, the same as a custom role. §6's closing summary was reworded to 'a conditional and often-zero file-list saving'.

suggestion: Replace the security row's `-10` cell with the actual range and its condition — e.g. `-10 to +10 files (min(matches,20) -> min(universe,10))` — and give the row two nets: `+~45` when 20 or more files matched, `+~55` at 10 matches, and worse below that, where the list grows. Add one sentence naming the per-file terms the column does not carry (a file read and a result row per file, as the section's first paragraph prices them), so a file-count delta is never read as a line-count delta.

finding: §2.5 defines `CodeFilesTotal` as the size of the *filtered* universe ("after the binary, fixture, and deleted drop rules, since a dropped file was never a candidate"), but no §7 item distinguishes that from the raw pre-filter universe. Item 10's `## Affected Files (10 of 34)` fixture exercises the field only where no file is dropped, so both readings render the same number and an implementation that totals `in.Universe` instead of `filterAuditUniverse(in)` passes every listed test. §7 item 17 exists precisely to close this hazard for the sibling field and even states the reasoning ("Without both cases an implementation that always uses the filtered universe passes") — the same reasoning is not applied to `CodeFilesTotal`, so the two new fields of §2.5 are guarded asymmetrically. The resulting bug is user-visible in the exact place §2.6 was added to stop lying: the header would report `(10 of 34)` counting binaries and `testdata/**` fixtures the auditor can never be shown.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 10 now carries a discriminating fixture: a universe holding both auditable files and files the drop rules remove (a testdata/ path, a .png) must report the post-drop count, so an implementation totalling the raw universe fails. Without it both readings of §2.5's definition render the same number.

suggestion: Extend §7 item 10 (or add an item) with a fixture whose universe contains files the drop rules remove — e.g. 12 code files plus a `.png` and a `testdata/x.go` — and assert the shared-arm header renders `(10 of 12)`, not `(10 of 14)`. State it in item 17's form: without a partially-dropped universe an implementation that totals the unfiltered universe passes.

finding: §3.2 and §3.3 pin eleven exact focus lines plus one exact `instructions` replacement ("only whether the code is maintainable and consistent with the conventions already present in this project"), but §7's only item covering §3 content — item 13 — is purely a *negative* blacklist of Go-isms. Nothing asserts the replacements landed. An implementation that deletes both `focus` arrays outright, or leaves the `instructions` clause truncated after removing the word `idiomatic`, passes item 13, passes item 15 (byte-identity between ejected files and the embedded corpus is content-agnostic), and passes the existing `TestDefaultCorpus_MatchesTable`, which asserts only that `Title` and `Instructions` are non-empty and never inspects `focus`. So the entire deliverable of §3 — the rewritten prompt content — has no pass/fail test, while the single line of §3.4 gets a verbatim assertion in item 15.

resolved.evidence: §7 gained a positive assertion item: security.json's focus equals the six §3.2 lines verbatim, maintainability-conventions.json's focus equals the five §3.3 lines verbatim, and its instructions contains the exact replacement clause. The finding's own argument is recorded in the item — item 13's blacklist alone passes against an emptied focus array.

suggestion: Add the positive half to item 13 (or a new item): assert `security.json` has 6 focus entries and `maintainability-conventions.json` has 5, each matching a distinguishing substring from §3.2/§3.3 (e.g. `released on all paths`, `empty catch`, `parameterizing or joining API`, `doc comment explaining intent`, `roughly 80 lines`), and that `maintainability-conventions.json`'s `instructions` contains the §3.3 replacement clause verbatim.

finding: §7 item 14 closes with "so every §4 requirement is guarded rather than only the first two", but two of its own clauses are not deterministically writable and two §4 requirements stay unguarded. (a) "no longer state `prompts[].role` as an enum of the three built-in ids" names no forbidden substring, and the two documents phrase it differently today — `skills/tp/SKILL.md:307` is prose ("is now one of `spec-coverage` / `security` / `maintainability-conventions`") while `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:398` is a table cell (``spec-coverage` \| `security` \| `maintainability-conventions``) — so two engineers invent two different forbidden strings, and a rewritten sentence that still names the ids as examples would fail one test and pass the other. (b) §4's "must not contain … any claim that `security` or `maintainability-conventions` receives its own file list or its own prompt section" is prose, not a substring, and no test can decide it. (c) The *positive* replacements §4 mandates are unasserted: REFERENCE.md must state the item id form `file-<role-id>-<slug>` (item 14 only forbids `file-sec-`, which passes if the line is deleted rather than corrected), and both documents must state that `prompts[].role` is any active role id from the corpus.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 14's unmechanizable clauses are replaced by substrings. It now requires REFERENCE.md to contain `file-<role-id>-<slug>` and both documents to contain `any active role id from the corpus`, while forbidding the old `always "implementation-auditor"` and the three-id enum rendering. Every §4 requirement is guarded by a required substring rather than by prose.

suggestion: Replace the two unwritable clauses with positive substring assertions, which subsume them: require `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md` to contain `file-<role-id>-<slug>`, and require both `REFERENCE.md` and `SKILL.md` to contain a pinned sentence such as `prompts[].role is any active role id from the corpus`. Then drop "no longer state … as an enum" and either drop §4's prose "any claim that …" clause or mark it explicitly as reviewer-checked rather than test-guarded, and correct item 14's closing claim accordingly.

finding: `enclosing_test` in `scripts/check-test-inventory.py` attributes a literal occurrence to the last `func Test…` declared before its byte offset — a positional heuristic, not a scope bound. Two consequences follow. An occurrence before the first test function in a file is silently discarded (`if test:` in `main`), and this repo puts its shared audit fixtures exactly there: `setupThreeRoleAudit` (internal/cli/audit_named_test.go:13-25), `auditPromptsByRole` and the `routingSpec` const (internal/cli/audit_routing_test.go, both above line 36). Symmetrically, a helper declared after a test credits its literals to that unrelated test and reports a false DRIFT with exit 1, which would block a round. §2.10 claims the check 'finds every committed Go test function referencing any of those literals'; it finds only those whose references happen to fall between two `func Test` declarations, which is precisely the placement the §2.8 rewrites are free to change.

resolved.evidence: Confirmed and fixed. enclosing_test attributes an occurrence to the last preceding `func Test`, so an occurrence in a package-level fixture declared before every test — setupThreeRoleAudit at audit_named_test.go:13 is exactly that — was silently discarded. Such occurrences are now collected per file and reported under the file name, and the run reports the count. Recorded as payment (4) in §2.10.

suggestion: Bound each test body at the next top-level `^func ` (test or not) rather than at the next `^func Test`, and report an occurrence outside every test function as a file-level reference naming the file, instead of dropping it.

finding: §2.4 closes with "Every role gets the same ordering, so no id is involved", but §2.1 keeps `spec-coverage` on "its own file selection" and §2.5 keeps that selection at `AuditFileCap` with its own `SpecCoverageTotal` — so `spec-coverage` never takes `selectCodeFiles`'s list and cannot get "the same ordering". As written the sentence asserts a property of a role the section does not touch, and the spec consequently never says whether the priority-substring ranking also applies to the spec-coverage selection (task-mapped set, or filtered universe in the no-task fallback). The tests do not settle it either: §7 item 3 pins only which roles emit and how many items, item 4 tests `selectCodeFiles`, and item 17 pins only `SpecCoverageTotal`'s two branches — so both readings pass.

resolved.evidence: §2.4's closing sentence was an unscoped universal. It now reads 'Every role taking the shared arm gets that same ordering, so no id selects a different one — spec-coverage is outside this sentence, since §2.1 keeps it on its own selection at AuditFileCap', which is what the section actually establishes.

suggestion: Scope the claim to the arm it describes ("Every role taking the shared arm gets the same ordering, so no id is involved") and add one clause stating explicitly that `spec-coverage`'s own selection is unchanged by §2.4 — or, if it is meant to be ranked too, say so and extend §7 item 17 with a membership assertion.

finding: §7 item 14 concludes "so every §4 requirement is guarded rather than only the first two", but two §4 requirements are positive statements that item 14 guards only by asserting the *old* text's absence: REFERENCE.md must document the item ids as `file-<role-id>-<slug>` (guarded only via the absence of `file-sec-`/`file-maint-`), and REFERENCE.md + SKILL.md must state that `prompts[].role` is any active role id from the corpus (guarded only via "no longer state `prompts[].role` as an enum of the three built-in ids"). Deleting either passage outright satisfies the guard while leaving the doc silent on the rule §4 requires it to state. That negative sub-assertion is also the one clause in item 14 expressed as a semantic property rather than a literal substring, unlike the four exact strings beside it, so how to assert it is left open.

resolved.evidence: Same guard gap as the tester's unmechanizable-guard-assertion finding, fixed together in §7 item 14: the two positive §4 requirements this finding named — REFERENCE.md's item-id form and the prompts[].role wording — are now each guarded by a required substring rather than only by the absence of the superseded text.

suggestion: Add the positive halves as substring assertions: REFERENCE.md contains `file-<role-id>-<slug>`, and both docs contain a §4-fixed phrase such as `any active role id from the corpus`. The absence checks then become hardening rather than the whole guard. Alternatively, soften item 14's closing sentence to name which §4 requirements are prose-only and deliberately unguarded.
